title: Are Mexicans Really Better Off Under Claudia Sheinbaum?
gist: Former central banker Guillermo Ortiz challenges Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum's claim that Mexicans are better off than in 2018, arguing that her headline poverty-reduction data (41.9% to 29.5%) look far less rosy against a holistic set of socioeconomic indicators.

insights.claim: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has cited a fall in Mexico's poverty rate from 41.9% in 2018 to 29.5% as evidence that Mexicans are economically better off.
insights.speaker: GUILLERMO ORTIZ
insights.so_what: The government's core political narrative rests on poverty data; any revision or contrary indicators matter for policy continuity and fiscal risk perception.
insights.locator: One year ago, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum

insights.claim: Mexico's government cites a cumulative 135% real increase in the minimum wage since the start of the 'Fourth Transformation' under Andrés Manuel López Obrador.
insights.speaker: GUILLERMO ORTIZ
insights.so_what: Aggressive real minimum-wage hikes affect labor costs for nearshoring manufacturers and consumer demand in Mexico.

insights.claim: Mexico's welfare-state benefits reach 32 million of the country's 133 million people, according to the government.
insights.speaker: GUILLERMO ORTIZ
insights.so_what: Welfare transfers covering roughly a quarter of the population are a sizable, politically sticky fiscal commitment.

insights.claim: A more holistic look at Mexico's socioeconomic data casts doubt on the government's claim that Mexicans are better off today than in 2018, despite falling extreme poverty.
insights.speaker: GUILLERMO ORTIZ
insights.so_what: Don't take headline poverty improvements at face value when assessing Mexico's growth and social stability; look at broader indicators.
insights.quote: a more holistic look at the available socioeconomic data casts doubt on that rosy picture
